analytics:compass-ai-practice-setup-funn.title: Compass AI practice setup — where setups stop
analytics:compass-ai-practice-setup-funn.excerpt: In the Compass AI practice setup flow, where every step is required, setups stop most at step 3 ("Connect calendar") and stay there longest, then at step 4 ("Invite your team"). This summary covers where setups stopped and for how long; it doesn't say why.

deliverable:mental-models/care-coordinat.title: Care Coordinators' Mental Model of Alert Ranking
deliverable:mental-models/care-coordinat.excerpt: The designer's paraphrase of the coordinator view: the system should defer to the coordinator's sense of a patient's history-driven risk — an experience-weighted judgment call. In 2025 this rested on one coordinator, P81: "I wanted to tell it 'no, this one's more urgent because I know this patient's history,' but there was nowhere to put that." It now rests on two team coordinators. In 2026, P81 said their most common reason for moving an alert is something the patient or a family member said on the phone that isn't in the chart yet, and P134, on a complex care team with a high-risk panel, said "half of deciding who's at risk is knowing what happened to them last winter" (both observed: what they said, not measured). Participants saw the ranking weight recency more heavily than their own sense of clinical risk; 4 of 5 disagreed with the AI's top-3 ranking on at least one of three test queues. There's no way for a coordinator's override to feed back into the ranking. Triage of a 20-item queue was still faster with the AI ranking than with a chronological queue in this simulated test (avg 6.5 min vs. 9 min).

deliverable:mental-models/compass-ai-sch.title: Practice and IT Administrators' Mental Model of Schedule Access and Staff Invites
deliverable:mental-models/compass-ai-sch.excerpt: What the build says each step does: Connect calendar is "read access to the practice's appointment schedule"; Invite your team "gives clinicians and staff access to Compass AI and sends them an email" (2026-02-03 session-notes.md:33-35 ). The screens don't list the fields read or say when the email is sent ( :46-47 , :52 ). At session setup the designer stated that the calendar step is required because the scribe attaches recordings to scheduled encounters ( :38 ); that is the designer's stated rationale, not something any session tested.

deliverable:mindsets/wants-to-know-what-.title: Wants to Know What a Step Commits Them To
deliverable:mindsets/wants-to-know-what-.excerpt: Not a persona: a stance that showed up in both roles in the 2026-02-03 usability test, Practice Administrators (P154-P157) and IT Administrators (P158, P159), at the two steps where setups stop most, Connect calendar and Invite your team ( raw/2026-01-20-dashboard-review-compass-ai-practice-setup-completion/session-notes.md:51-56 ). Both steps reach beyond the setup screen: one gives Compass AI read access to the practice's appointment schedule, the other gives staff access and sends them an email (2026-02-03 session-notes.md:33-35 ). At each, participants wanted to know what the step would set off and whether someone else's part was in place before they committed to it. This is about admin setup of Compass AI, not staff training.

deliverable:wireframes/ambient-scribe-me.title: Ambient Scribe — Sound-Alike Medication Flag
deliverable:wireframes/ambient-scribe-me.excerpt:
Placement: inline, immediately after the medication name — tested 5:1 over a right-hand margin badge, since participants didn't want to look away from the text.
Visual treatment: small amber pill-shaped badge, distinct in shape and color from the existing subtle low-confidence underline, so the two signals are never visually conflated.
Copy: short on-hover/on-tap label — "Possible sound-alike medication name — verify before signing" — worded to prompt verification, not to assert an error.

finding:ambient-scribe#0.title: Ambient AI Scribe
finding:ambient-scribe#0.excerpt:
The ambient AI scribe has moved from a formative concept (v0.1, Feb 2025) through iteration (v0.2, Sep 2025) to a GA release candidate (Jan 2026). 3 of the original 5 participants returned for v0.2, and at least one (P09) also took part in the GA-candidate round, for longitudinal comparison.
PHI handling: The critical draft-retention/audit gap found in v0.1 was fixed by v0.2 and has remained stable through the GA candidate — drafts auto-expire after 10 minutes of inactivity and the behavior is documented for Compliance. No PHI-handling issues have recurred since.

finding:ambient-scribe#12.title: Ambient AI Scribe
finding:ambient-scribe#12.section: Since GA: 2026 Physician, NP and PA Interviews
finding:ambient-scribe#12.excerpt: Session lock on shared workstations. One Nurse Practitioner (primary care) is locked out when the idle timeout fires while they are at the exam table, "most afternoons, at least once"; the widget shows no message, and they re-authenticate and scroll through the draft before saying more (2026-04-28, HIGH). Because they don't know what happens to an in-progress draft if a colleague signs in on the shared workstation during a lock, they stop the scribe before leaving the room, which splits one visit across several recordings (2026-04-28, HIGH). The paused state has not shipped.

finding:ambient-scribe#13.title: Ambient AI Scribe
finding:ambient-scribe#13.section: Since GA: 2026 Physician, NP and PA Interviews
finding:ambient-scribe#13.excerpt: Opting in. One Physician (Internal Medicine resident) did not opt in at GA: writing their own notes was how they worked out their assessment while learning, and they did not describe doubt about the draft's accuracy as a reason (2026-10-08, MEDIUM). They opted in "about three months into clinic" and for a new problem write the assessment themselves, or rewrite the draft's assessment before signing (2026-10-08, MEDIUM). One resident's account can't explain the attending/resident adoption gap in the 2026-01-27 dashboard review.

finding:ambient-scribe#9.title: Ambient AI Scribe
finding:ambient-scribe#9.section: Since GA: 2026 Physician, NP and PA Interviews
finding:ambient-scribe#9.excerpt: Medication lines. One Physician (Family Medicine) checks every medication change in the plan against the order they placed, underlined or not, and rewrites changes worded as discussed rather than decided (2026-03-24, HIGH); they recalled one sound-alike name since GA, glyburide written where glipizide had been said, which was underlined, one recollection and not a rate (2026-03-24, MEDIUM). One Physician (Rheumatology) reads the whole medication section of long lists to find the one or two lines that changed (2026-06-30, HIGH), rewrites dose schedules the draft writes incompletely, such as a prednisone taper that keeps only its first step, which they put at "a few times a month", or a methotrexate dose without "weekly" (2026-06-30, HIGH), and checks whether each dose is the patient's report or their own decision (2026-06-30, MEDIUM). The distinct medication flag has not shipped; both accounts describe drafts with the confidence underline only.

finding:ambient-scribe-post-ga-refinemen.title: Ambient Scribe — Post-GA Refinements
finding:ambient-scribe-post-ga-refinemen.excerpt: In a 6-person concept test, a distinct sound-alike-medication flag was recognized as different from generic confidence highlighting. The GA-candidate round treated sound-alike medication errors as an ongoing monitoring item, relying on the general confidence-highlighted variant to surface them. A concept test of a dedicated, visually distinct flag found 5 of 6 participants correctly recognized it as categorically different from generic low confidence — but also surfaced a new risk: 2 of 6 participants said the flag's specificity made them trust unflagged medication lines more than they should. Any rollout needs to actively counter that over-trust framing, not just ship the flag.

finding:ambient-scribe-post-ga-refinemen.title: Ambient Scribe — Post-GA Refinements
finding:ambient-scribe-post-ga-refinemen.excerpt: Session lock during active dictation currently reads as silent data loss, even though it isn't. The locked state's interaction with an in-progress recording was flagged as unresolved in encounter-view 's own notes, sourced from a May 2025 SSO/MFA interview side comment. Direct observation confirms the practical impact: all 4 shadowed clinicians assumed a locked session had destroyed their draft and restarted dictation from scratch, even though the draft is preserved server-side. IT Security confirmed the 10-minute idle-timeout policy itself is fixed, but an explicit "paused, draft preserved" state is a UI-only fix, not a policy change.

finding:care-coordination-triage#12.title: Care Coordination & Alert Triage
finding:care-coordination-triage#12.excerpt: Still open after the 2026 interviews: how often the after-visit summary misses changes; whether the 2025 queue showed coordinators what its ranking was based on; how accurate the ranking is; real-world triage speed; how often coordinators follow a ranked order without judgement (no measurement of rubber-stamping); and whether the override-capture idea reached the data-science team.

finding:clinician-experience-documentati.title: Clinician Experience & Documentation Burden
finding:clinician-experience-documentati.excerpt:
Three sessions trace clinician sentiment and documentation burden across the year: a nursing attitudes survey (Feb 2025, before AI framing was introduced), a clinician dashboard usability test (May 2025), and an org-wide burnout/documentation-burden baseline survey (Sep 2025, which explicitly referenced the AI initiative).
The top volunteered concern was not accuracy or privacy — it was voice. In February, "losing my clinical narrative voice / it will sound robotic" was the most common open-ended concern among nurses — not accuracy or privacy as originally hypothesized.

finding:clinician-experience-documentati.title: Clinician Experience & Documentation Burden
finding:clinician-experience-documentati.excerpt: Documentation burden is real and quantifiable, not just anecdotal. The September baseline found documentation burden is physicians' #1 self-selected burnout driver (52%, ahead of patient volume at 31%), with 64% doing regular after-hours "pajama time" charting (avg. 1.2 hrs/day). The session recommends it as the official pre-AI baseline for measuring Compass AI's impact at 6 and 12 months post-rollout. Caveat: the September survey mentioned the AI initiative explicitly in its framing, while the February survey didn't — any comparison between the two datasets needs to account for that framing difference, not treat them as a clean before/after.

finding:compass-ai-practice-setup#0.title: Compass AI Practice Setup
finding:compass-ai-practice-setup#0.excerpt: Three early-2026 sessions look at how an administrator sets Compass AI up for a practice: a dashboard review of setups (Jan 2026), a moderated usability test of the setup flow with 4 Practice Administrators and 2 IT Administrators (Feb 2026), and an interview with an IT Administrator who approves access requests across practices (Feb 2026). This is about admin setup of Compass AI, not staff training; elsewhere in the corpus "onboarding" can mean training copy for clinicians ( raw/2026-02-10-ambient-scribe-medication-flag-concept/session-notes.md:62 ).

finding:prior-authorization#0.title: AI-Assisted Prior Authorization
finding:prior-authorization#0.excerpt:
AI-drafted prior authorization justifications were tested in two rounds (v1, Apr 2025; v2, Nov 2025) with the same utilization review nurse supervisor across both, which mattered for tracking whether fixes actually landed.
v1 surfaced a correctness bug (citing outdated diagnosis codes) serious enough that participants said it would likely cause payer denials — not a UX problem, a data-freshness/model fix. It also surfaced a durable requirement: nurses want inline citations to the specific chart text behind each suggestion ("show your work"), not just a black-box draft.

finding:scope-boundaries-and-workflow-fi.title: Scope Boundaries & Workflow Fit
finding:scope-boundaries-and-workflow-fi.excerpt: By Feb 2026, IT Security confirmed the 10-minute idle timeout is not adjustable per feature (2026-02-17-session-lock-during-dictation/session-notes.md:49-50; see [ambient-scribe-post-ga-refinements.md](ambient-scribe-post-ga-refinements.md)). Objective
Understand executive priorities, risk tolerance, and success criteria for the Compass AI modernization program before any tools are scoped.
Method
Method: 1:1 stakeholder interview (60 min, recorded w/ consent, transcript scrubbed)
Researcher: J. Alvarez
Full participant roster: see participants.md in this folder
Key Findings
[HIGH] (risk tolerance) Both stakeholders want AI pilots to start in low-PHI-exposure workflows (scheduling, intake) before touching clinical documentation, citing HIPAA audit exposure as the top concern.
[MEDIUM] (success criteria) VP Clinical Informatics defines success as 'reduced documentation time,' while CIO defines success as 'reduced vendor sprawl' — the two are not currently reconciled in a shared metric.
[MEDIUM] (governance) Neither stakeholder could name who owns model-output accuracy sign-off; assumed it would 'probably fall to compliance.'
[LOW] (change management) Both anticipate clinician skepticism based on a prior failed CDS (clinical decision support) alert rollout in 2022.
Representative Quotes
"We can't be the org that leaks PHI through some vendor's training pipeline. That's the headline we're trying to avoid, not chase." — Chief Information Officer, P01
"If a doctor spends less time typing and more time looking at the patient, I don't care what's under the hood." — VP Clinical Informatics, P02
Recommendations
Facilitate a follow-up session to align on 2-3 shared, measurable success metrics before scoping any pilot.
Document a RACI for AI-output review/sign-off; surface the gap to Compliance directly.
Reference the 2022 CDS alert rollout retro in early clinician-facing research to avoid repeating known failure modes.
Follow-ups / Open Questions
Who in Compliance should own model-output sign-off? Schedule follow-up interview.
Request access to 2022 CDS alert rollout post-mortem if it exists.

raw:2025-04-08-usability-test-prior-auth.title: Usability Test — AI-Assisted Prior Authorization Drafting (v1)
raw:2025-04-08-usability-test-prior-auth.participants: Participants: 4 — Utilization Review Nurse, Utilization Review Nurse (supervisor)
raw:2025-04-08-usability-test-prior-auth.excerpt:
Objective
Test whether an AI-drafted prior authorization request (pulling from chart data to pre-fill medical necessity justification) speeds up the process without introducing errors that could cause denials.
Method
Method: Moderated usability test, 4 realistic case scenarios, 60 min/session
Researcher: Priya Patel
Full participant roster: see participants.md in this folder
Key Findings
[HIGH] (accuracy) In 2 of 4 cases, the AI draft cited outdated diagnosis codes still present elsewhere in the chart rather than the most recent/active ones, which participants said would likely cause a payer denial if submitted as-is.
[HIGH] (liability concern) The supervisor was firm that nurses would still need to read every AI-drafted justification in full before submission, since a wrongly submitted prior auth can delay patient care by days — no shortcut is acceptable here.
[HIGH] (time savings (positive)) Despite the above, participants estimated the draft cut initial drafting time from ~15 minutes to ~5 minutes per straightforward case when the citation was correct, which was seen as a real win if accuracy improves.
[MEDIUM] (transparency) Participants wanted to see which specific chart entries the AI pulled from, inline, rather than trusting a black-box summary — 'show your work' was mentioned unprompted by 3 of 4.
Representative Quotes
"Five minutes saved is great until it's the case that gets denied and now I'm on the phone with the payer for 40 minutes instead. Show me where it got that info." — Utilization Review Nurse, P17
"I actually really liked this for the boring, obvious cases. Just don't let it near the complicated ones yet." — Utilization Review Nurse, P19
Recommendations
Fix the outdated-diagnosis-code issue before any further piloting; this is a correctness bug, not a UX issue.
Add inline source citations (chart entry + date) for every claim in the generated justification.
Consider limiting initial pilot scope to 'straightforward' case types the nurses themselves can help define, deferring complex cases.
Follow-ups / Open Questions
Work with engineering to confirm whether the outdated-code issue is a data-freshness bug or a model retrieval issue.
Ask supervisor to help define what counts as a 'straightforward' case for a narrower v2 pilot scope.

raw:2025-05-20-interview-it-security-sso.title: Interview — IT Security on SSO/MFA Modernization Impact
raw:2025-05-20-interview-it-security-sso.excerpt:
Objective
Understand planned SSO/MFA changes and their anticipated impact on clinical workflow before any AI feature is layered on top of authentication-dependent sessions.
Method
Method: 1:1 interview, 40 min
Researcher: Priya Patel
Full participant roster: see participants.md in this folder
Key Findings
[HIGH] (session timeout) Planned MFA rollout would introduce a shared-workstation re-authentication requirement every 15 minutes, down from the current 4 hours — flagged internally as likely to cause clinician pushback based on prior rollout feedback, independent of any AI feature.
[MEDIUM] (badge-tap workflow) Most units already use badge-tap proximity login for shared workstations; new MFA plan hasn't yet been confirmed to work with the existing badge-tap hardware.
[MEDIUM] (AI session risk) If an AI ambient scribe session is mid-recording when a forced re-auth occurs, current design has no defined behavior — could lose the in-progress draft.
Representative Quotes
"Security wants 15 minutes, clinical ops wants 4 hours, and nobody's told me yet who wins that argument, but I have to build for one of them." — IT Security Engineer, P31
"Nobody's asked what happens to an active AI recording session if the screen locks mid-visit. That's going to be a real incident the first time it happens." — IT Security Engineer, P31
Recommendations
Flag the ambient-scribe-mid-recording + forced-reauth interaction to the ambient scribe engineering team immediately as an unhandled edge case.
Push for a joint decision meeting between Security and Clinical Ops on the session timeout conflict before MFA rollout, independent of Compass AI.
Follow-ups / Open Questions
Confirm badge-tap hardware compatibility with new MFA plan.
Get the ambient scribe team's answer on session-loss behavior into a future usability test script.

raw:2025-10-21-interview-training-depart.title: Interview — Training & Education Dept on Rollout/Change Management Planning
raw:2025-10-21-interview-training-depart.participants: Participants: 1 — Director of Clinical Training & Education ×1
raw:2025-10-21-interview-training-depart.excerpt:
Objective
Understand what a realistic training/rollout plan looks like for the first Compass AI features going to general availability, drawing on lessons from past rollouts.
Method
Method: 1:1 interview, 40 min
Researcher: Priya Patel
Full participant roster: see participants.md in this folder
Key Findings
[MEDIUM] (past rollout lesson) Director pointed to the 2022 CDS alert rollout (also referenced by executives in January) as a cautionary tale specifically because training was a single 20-minute video with no hands-on practice, and adoption suffered as a result — she wants any Compass AI rollout to include live, hands-on sessions instead.
[MEDIUM] (champion model) Prefers a 'unit champion' model (1-2 respected staff per unit trained early and deeply, who then support peers) over an all-at-once broadcast rollout, based on past success with an unrelated EHR module rollout in 2023.
[LOW] (timing sensitivity) Flagged that rolling out during flu season (Nov-Feb) has historically correlated with poor training attendance and should be avoided if possible for the ambient scribe GA rollout.

"We already know what doesn't work. A video nobody watches and hoping for the best. I don't want to repeat 2022." — Director of Clinical Training & Education, P99
"Give me two respected nurses per unit, trained early and given actual time to practice, and they'll do more for adoption than any all-staff email ever will." — Director of Clinical Training & Education, P99
Recommendations
Build the ambient scribe GA rollout plan around the unit-champion model, and explicitly avoid flu-season timing given the historical attendance pattern.
Include hands-on practice time in training, not just a recorded overview, directly addressing the 2022 lesson learned.
Follow-ups / Open Questions
Get the actual 2022 CDS rollout adoption numbers if they exist, to quantify the lesson rather than rely on recollection.
Identify candidate unit champions once the GA rollout unit list is finalized.

Objective
Final validation pass on the ambient scribe before GA release, testing the v0.3 confidence-indicator concept (from September's recommendation) and confirming readiness against the full history of prior findings.
Method
Method: Moderated usability test, simulated + 2 real (consented) low-acuity encounters, 45 min/session
Researcher: Priya Patel
Full participant roster: see participants.md in this folder

Objective
The 2026-01-20 dashboard review found setups of Compass AI for a practice stopping most at Connect calendar (7 of 24 setups started) and then at Invite your team (3 of 24), and said a dashboard can't show why ( 2026-01-20-dashboard-review-compass-ai-practice-setup-completion/session-notes.md:45-46,72 ). Method
Method: Moderated usability test, remote, think-aloud, 60 min/session, one participant per session
Researcher: Priya Patel (moderator)
Full participant roster: see participants.md in this folder
Participants: 6 — 4 Practice Administrators (P154-P157) and 2 IT Administrators (P158, P159)
Steps tested, in order: 1 Sign in with Meridian SSO; 2 Practice details; 3 Connect calendar (read access to the practice's appointment schedule); 4 Invite your team (gives clinicians and staff access to Compass AI and sends them an email); 5 Review & finish.
Build: Steps 3 and 4 are required in this build. There is no "Connect later" and no "Skip for now"; the only way past each step is to complete it.
Design context: At session setup, the designer, Sam Okafor, stated that the calendar step is required because the scribe attaches recordings to scheduled encounters.
Test environment: Participants signed in with their own Meridian SSO and were asked to set up as they would for their own practice. The environment was a test one: step 3 connected to a prepared sandbox calendar standing in for the practice's schedule, and step 4 used a prepared test staff list, so no real schedule was read and no real staff were emailed.
Test accommodation: When a participant stopped at step 3, the moderator told them it was the sandbox calendar and let them continue. Every participant completed step 3 this way or on their own, so completing step 3 in this session is not a result.
Not covered: The step 4 screen doesn't say when the invite email is sent, and these notes don't record when this build sends it. How Compass AI access is provisioned (through SSO groups or through these invites) wasn't known to the moderator and isn't recorded in the corpus.

[HIGH] (calendar: who can approve) 3 of 4 Practice Administrators (P154, P155, P157) stopped at Connect calendar and wouldn't connect it: it gives Compass AI access to patient appointments, and they did not think they could approve that. Each said it was IT's decision. The fourth (P156) asked the moderator whether connecting the schedule was theirs to approve before going on. All 4 continued only on the sandbox calendar (see Test accommodation).
[MEDIUM] (calendar: what is read) Both IT Administrators (P158, P159) connected the calendar, but only after asking which fields are read (for example, whether visit reasons are included). The screen doesn't list them; the moderator couldn't answer, and both went on without an answer.
[HIGH] (invite: timing and training) 3 of 4 Practice Administrators (P154, P156, P157) hesitated at Invite your team. They weren't sure whether the email goes out when they finish the step or at Review & finish, and they didn't want staff emailed before champion training is booked for the practice. P155 entered the test staff list and went on without comment.
[MEDIUM] (invite: provisioning) One IT Administrator (P159) asked whether the invites create accounts or rely on the SSO groups staff are already in. The moderator couldn't answer, and the corpus doesn't record how access is provisioned.
[LOW] (sign in and practice details) No issues at Sign in or Practice details: 6 of 6 participants completed both without help or comment on a problem.

"Before I connect it I want to know what it pulls. Times and providers, fine. Visit reasons, that's a different conversation." — IT Administrator, P158
"Does this make them an account, or does it just use the groups they're already in? Because if it's a separate list, I'm the one keeping it in sync." — IT Administrator, P159

List the fields read from the appointment schedule on the Connect calendar step.
Add a "Send to IT for approval" path on Connect calendar for an administrator who can't approve the access themselves.
Say on the Invite your team screen when the invite email is sent.
Let administrators schedule the invite email for a date, so it can go out once training is booked.

raw:2026-02-10-ambient-scribe-medication.title: Usability Test — Ambient Scribe Sound-Alike Medication Flag Concept
raw:2026-02-10-ambient-scribe-medication.excerpt:
Objective
The GA-candidate round (2026-01-13) recommended treating sound-alike medication errors as an ongoing post-GA monitoring item rather than a launch blocker, since the existing confidence-highlighted variant already surfaces them as generically low-confidence. This session tests an early concept that goes one step further: a distinct flag specifically for suspected sound-alike medication names, visually separate from the general low-confidence underline, to see whether participants notice and act on it differently than they do on ordinary low-confidence text.
Method
Method: Moderated usability test, 6 simulated encounters seeded with known sound-alike pairs (e.g. hydralazine/hydroxyzine, clonidine/Klonopin), 40 min/session
Researcher: Priya Patel
Full participant roster: see participants.md in this folder
Key Findings
[HIGH] (flag recognized correctly) 5 of 6 participants correctly identified the medication-specific flag (a distinct amber pill-shaped badge, vs. the generic low-confidence underline) as "different from the usual low-confidence thing" within the first two encounters, without being told the distinction existed.
[MEDIUM] (over-trust risk) 2 participants said the badge's specificity made them more likely to treat unflagged medication lines as automatically correct — the opposite of the intended effect, and worth watching as adoption scales.
[LOW] (placement) Badge placement inline with the medication name (vs. in a right-hand margin, tested as an alternate) was preferred 5:1 — participants didn't want to look away from the text to check a flag.
[LOW] (false positive tolerance) One deliberately-seeded false positive (a real but unusual drug name) was accepted by all 6 participants as "worth a second look, not annoying" — suggests some over-flagging is tolerable if the badge is visually light.
Representative Quotes
"That's different from the fuzzy-underline stuff — this one's telling me specifically 'check the drug name,' which is exactly what I'd want flagged." — Physician, Internal Medicine, P22
"If it's not flagged, I might just... trust it more than I should. That's on me, but it's worth knowing the tool does that to people." — Nurse Practitioner, P24
Recommendations
Build the distinct medication-safety flag as its own variant, inline with the medication name, separate from generic confidence highlighting.
Before rollout, pair the flag with brief onboarding copy or training-pilot messaging that explicitly counters the over-trust-on-unflagged-lines risk surfaced by 2 of 6 participants — don't let the flag imply "anything unflagged is guaranteed correct."
Feed the false-positive tolerance finding to whoever tunes the sound-alike detection threshold — participants have headroom for a few extra false positives in exchange for not missing a real one.
Follow-ups / Open Questions
Needs a larger-N validation pass before this moves from concept test to build-ready spec.
Over-trust-on-unflagged risk should be checked again once the post-GA monitoring dashboard (recommended 2026-01-13) has real error-rate data to compare against self-reported behavior.

raw:2026-02-17-session-lock-during-dicta.excerpt:
Objective
encounter-view.md 's component notes flag the locked state's interaction with an in-progress ambient scribe recording as an open edge case, raised as a side note in the 2025-05-20 SSO/MFA interview but never directly studied. This session shadows clinicians through their normal SSO/MFA idle-timeout window while actively dictating, to observe what actually happens today and what they expect/want instead.
Method
Method: Contextual inquiry / shadowing, 5 clinicians observed through at least one natural idle-timeout event during a real or simulated dictation session, plus 1 IT Security stakeholder interviewed on the technical constraints
Researcher: Priya Patel
Full participant roster: see participants.md in this folder
Key Findings
[CRITICAL] (silent draft loss) In the current build, a session lock mid-recording simply freezes the ambient-scribe widget with no message; 4 of 5 clinicians assumed the draft was lost and started re-dictating from scratch after re-authenticating, even though the draft is server-side and actually survives the lock.
[HIGH] (no explicit paused state) There is no visual distinction between "recording," "frozen because locked," and "actually stopped" — participants could not tell which state they were in without asking a shadowing observer.
[MEDIUM] (re-auth friction stacks) Clinicians already re-authenticate frequently for unrelated reasons (badge-tap SSO renewals); a lock during dictation is perceived as "one more annoying re-login," not as a distinct, expected safety behavior — this framing gap likely drives the abandon-and-redictate behavior above as much as the missing UI does.
[LOW] (IT Security confirms feasibility) IT Security confirmed the 10-minute idle timeout is not adjustable per-feature, but confirmed an explicit "paused, draft preserved" UI state is technically straightforward to add without changing the timeout policy itself.
Representative Quotes
"I genuinely thought I'd lost it. I've just gotten used to starting over when the screen locks, so I didn't even try to check." — Physician, Family Medicine, P31
"If it said 'paused, nothing lost, just log back in,' I'd believe it and wait. Right now it just looks broken." — Nurse Practitioner, P33
"The timeout window itself is a hard policy constraint, but what the screen tells the clinician during that window is entirely a product decision — that part isn't locked down." — IT Security stakeholder
Recommendations
Add an explicit "paused — draft preserved, re-authenticate to resume" state to the encounter-view / ambient-scribe-widget lock interaction, replacing the current silent freeze.
Do not attempt to change or extend the idle-timeout policy itself — per IT Security, treat it as fixed and solve this entirely at the UI-messaging layer.
Pair the new state with brief messaging that reframes the lock as an expected safety behavior rather than an unrelated login interruption, to counter the "one more annoying re-login" framing found here.
Follow-ups / Open Questions
Confirm with IT Security whether the same "paused, preserved" messaging pattern should extend to other session-timeout-adjacent surfaces beyond ambient scribe.
Re-test the abandon-and-redictate behavior once the explicit paused state ships, to confirm it actually changes clinician behavior and not just their stated understanding.

raw:2026-03-03-interview-care-coordinato.title: Interview — Care Coordinator on Chart Review of Scribe-Drafted Notes
raw:2026-03-03-interview-care-coordinato.excerpt:
Objective
Two months after the ambient scribe went GA in January 2026, understand how pre-outreach chart review has changed for a care coordinator now that many of the visit notes they read are scribe-drafted, and whether the "what changed since last review" idea from the January 2025 baseline still describes what they need. Care coordinators don't use the scribe themselves; they read the signed notes clinicians produce with it.
Method
Method: 1:1 interview, 45 min
Researcher: Priya Patel
Full participant roster: see participants.md in this folder
Context: The participant is a care coordinator on an ambulatory primary care team who makes outreach calls to a panel of patients and reviews each chart before calling. They did not take part in the January 2025 baseline or the August 2025 alert-triage test. The chart-review summary panel ("what changed since last review") is still a concept and hasn't been built; they were described the idea in this session, not shown screens.
Key Findings
[HIGH] (scribe-drafted notes) Since GA, the visit notes they read before an outreach call are longer and more conversational than the notes clinicians used to type. What they need for the call (the plan, follow-up items, medication changes) is in there but takes longer to find, so they now jump straight to the plan and the medication list and only read the rest if something there doesn't make sense. They put the extra time at "a couple of extra minutes" on complex patients. This is their informal impression, not something timed in this session.
[MEDIUM] (what changed) Without being prompted with the January 2025 quote, they asked for a view of "what changed since my last outreach call". They anchored it on their own last contact with the patient, not on the patient's last visit, because a patient may have had several visits, results or medication changes since the coordinator last spoke with them. This refines the "what changed since last review" concept: the reference point that matters to them is the coordinator's last contact.
Representative Quotes
"The notes are longer now. It's all in there, it just reads like a conversation, so I skip to the plan and the med list and work backwards if I have to." — Care Coordinator, P130
"I don't need to know what happened at the last visit. I need to know what happened since the last time I talked to them." — Care Coordinator, P130
Recommendations
Anchor the chart-review summary concept on the coordinator's last outreach contact, not only on the last visit, and test both anchors when the concept is next put in front of coordinators.
Share with the ambient scribe team that downstream readers who aren't clinicians (coordinators, as well as coders) rely on the plan and medication sections being easy to find in scribe-drafted notes.
Follow-ups / Open Questions
How much longer chart review takes on scribe-drafted notes is not measured. The January 2025 baseline's 8-14 minutes per patient hasn't been re-timed since GA; a timed observation would be needed to check the "couple of extra minutes" impression.
Does "last outreach contact" exist as a recorded event anywhere a summary could read it, or only in the coordinator's own notes and the shared spreadsheet?

raw:2026-03-10-interview-medical-coder-c.title: Interview — Medical Coder on Coding from AI-Drafted Notes
raw:2026-03-10-interview-medical-coder-c.excerpt:
Objective
Two months after the ambient scribe went GA in January 2026, understand how coding from scribe-drafted notes differs from coding notes the physician typed, and what a coder would expect from the AI coding-suggestion concept (tested as a prototype in July 2025, not built or piloted) now that much of the documentation it would read is itself AI-drafted.
Method
Method: 1:1 interview, 45 min
Researcher: Priya Patel
Full participant roster: see participants.md in this folder
Context: Participant codes outpatient and some inpatient encounters daily and has coded from scribe-drafted notes since GA. They did not take part in the July 2025 usability test; their view of the coding-suggestion concept comes from a walkthrough of the July 2025 screens during this session.
Key Findings
[HIGH] (documentation gaps) Scribe-drafted notes often capture what was discussed in the visit but leave out the specificity coding depends on: laterality, acute vs. chronic, type or stage (they gave heart failure type and CKD stage as examples), and the "due to" link between two conditions. When it's missing the coder has two options, query the physician or code to the unspecified level, and they said they are doing both more often than with notes physicians typed from their own templates. They noted the July 2025 prototype's mismatches were mostly at the specificity level too, and expect a suggester reading these notes to hit the same wall.
[MEDIUM] (trust in AI-drafted notes) Nothing in the signed note shows which sentences the scribe drafted and which the physician typed or edited. When a sentence looks off (e.g., a diagnosis in the assessment that nothing else in the note supports), the coder can't tell whether it's a documentation problem worth a query or something the scribe picked up from the conversation that the physician didn't catch at sign-off. They weren't asking for a marker on the permanent chart, just "something I can see while I'm coding".
[MEDIUM] (query volume) Coder's impression is that queries back to physicians have gone up since GA, and that physicians are slower to answer queries about notes "they didn't really write". This is qualitative only: they had no count, and no department query data was reviewed in this session.
Representative Quotes
"I'm coding off what the doctor says happened. Now I read a sentence and I honestly don't know if the doctor said it or the scribe thing filled it in. Who wrote this? I can't tell you, and I'm the one putting a code on it." — Medical Coder (certified), P120
"If the suggester is reading the same notes I'm reading, it's going to land on unspecified too. It'll just get there faster than me." — Medical Coder (certified), P120
Recommendations
Collect the specificity elements coders most often query on scribe-drafted notes (laterality, acuity, type/stage, condition linkage) and share them with the ambient scribe team as input to the drafting prompts and note structure.
For the coding-suggestion concept, design for under-specified input: when the note doesn't support a specific code, the tool should say so rather than quietly suggest the unspecified code.
Raise with Compliance whether scribe-drafted vs. clinician-edited provenance could be shown in the coding view only, consistent with the CMIO's August 2025 model of no marker on the permanent chart.
Follow-ups / Open Questions
Get actual physician query counts from HIM leadership for the months before and after GA, to check the coder's impression.
Find out whether the scribe's generation metadata is captured at sentence level, and whether it could reach the coding workflow at all.

raw:2026-03-19-interview-primary-care-ph.title: Interview — Primary Care Physician on Incidental Content in Scribe Drafts
raw:2026-03-19-interview-primary-care-ph.excerpt:
Objective
Earlier ambient-scribe research looked at what the scribe gets wrong: medication dosages and sound-alike drug names, and whether clinicians trust the draft enough to skim it. Two sessions touched on what the scribe takes in more broadly. In an October 2025 contextual inquiry, a behavioral health clinician said that any AI tool listening to or drafting behavioral health session notes raises consent and 42 CFR Part 2 questions (2025-10-07-contextual-inquiry-behavioral-health-sensitive-notes/session-notes.md:28); the exclusion of that population from the near-term ambient scribe rollout is recorded in the scope-boundaries finding (scope-boundaries-and-workflow-fit.md:72-74). A care coordinator said the visit notes they read since GA are longer and more conversational than the notes clinicians used to type (2026-03-03-interview-care-coordinator-chart-review-scribe-notes/session-notes.md:31). Neither asked the person signing a draft about content the scribe writes down correctly but that doesn't belong in a visit note: small talk, a patient's remarks about other people, side conversations with a family member in the room. This session asked a primary care physician, two months after the January 2026 GA, what of that kind ends up in their drafts and what they remove before they sign.
Method
Method: 1:1 interview, 45 min
Researcher: Priya Patel
Full participant roster: see participants.md in this folder
Context: The participant is an internal medicine physician in an ambulatory primary care clinic, mid-career. They opted in to the ambient scribe after the January 2026 GA and use it for most of their visits. The scribe drafts visit notes for physicians, NPs and PAs; the clinician reviews the draft, corrects single lines in place, and signs. Low-confidence transcription is shown with a subtle underline. They did not take part in any earlier session. This is an interview about their own practice; nothing was shown or observed.
Key Findings
[HIGH] (incidental content) Their drafts regularly contain things that were said in the room but that they would not have written themselves: small talk at the start of the visit, a patient's remarks about a relative's health, comments made by a family member who came to the visit, and their own asides ("let me pull up your labs"). They remove these line by line with the in-place edit before signing. They put it at "most visits, a line or two", an informal impression, not a count.
[MEDIUM] (not underlined) The underline marks lines where the scribe was unsure what it heard. Incidental content is usually transcribed accurately, so it is not underlined, and nothing in the draft points them to it. It also doesn't land in a predictable section: they have found it in the history of present illness and in the social history. To catch it they read the whole draft, including sections where nothing is underlined. That is one physician's practice; whether others do the same is not known.
[MEDIUM] (judgement) What counts as incidental is a judgement call. A remark about stress at home can be clinically relevant and stay in the note; the same remark in passing about someone else is removed. They would not want the scribe to remove anything on its own. They could see value in it pointing out lines that might not belong, as long as they decide. That is an expectation; nothing was shown.
Representative Quotes
"It writes down everything that was said, not everything that matters. The sister's surgery is in my note until I take it out." — Physician (Internal Medicine), P146
"The underline tells me where it wasn't sure what it heard. It heard the small talk perfectly, so nothing tells me to look there." — Physician (Internal Medicine), P146
Recommendations
Share with the ambient scribe team that the confidence underline doesn't help with incidental content, because that content is usually transcribed accurately; reviewing for it means reading the whole draft.
If anything is designed for this, explore pointing out lines that may not belong in the note rather than removing them, so the clinician makes the call.
Keep this separate from the transcription-confidence work: it is about what belongs in the note, not whether it was heard correctly.
Follow-ups / Open Questions
How often drafts contain incidental content is not measured; "most visits, a line or two" is one physician's impression.
Whether other physicians, NPs and PAs remove the same kinds of content, and how long it takes them, is not known; this is one interview.
What happens to text a clinician removes before signing is not recorded in the corpus and was not discussed in this session.

raw:2026-03-24-interview-family-physicia.excerpt:
Objective
Earlier ambient-scribe sessions tested medication accuracy in drafts: dosage errors in v0.1 and v0.2, sound-alike drug names at the GA release candidate, and a concept for a distinct sound-alike medication flag (2026-02-10). The plan section has so far come up only from the reader's side: a care coordinator goes straight to the plan and the medication list in the visit notes they read before an outreach call (2026-03-03-interview-care-coordinator-chart-review-scribe-notes/session-notes.md:31, :43), and the 2026-03-17 clinic nurse interview (2026-03-17-interview-clinic-nurse-reading-scribe-drafted-notes) heard that plan items sometimes land in the body of the note rather than the plan (2026-03-17-interview-clinic-nurse-reading-scribe-drafted-notes/session-notes.md:30). None of those sessions asked the person who signs the draft how they check the plan section, where decisions made during the visit, including medication changes, are supposed to end up. This session asked a family physician, two months after the January 2026 GA, how they check the plan and the medication lines in a draft before they sign.
Method
Method: 1:1 interview, 45 min
Researcher: Priya Patel
Full participant roster: see participants.md in this folder
Context: The participant is a family medicine physician in an ambulatory primary care clinic, mid-career. They opted in to the ambient scribe after the January 2026 GA. The scribe drafts the visit note only; the clinician enters orders, including medication orders, separately. Low-confidence transcription is shown with a subtle underline. The distinct sound-alike medication flag tested on 2026-02-10 has not shipped; there is no distinct medication marking beyond the confidence underline. They did not take part in any earlier session. This is an interview about their own practice; nothing was shown or observed.
Key Findings
[HIGH] (plan section) When a decision is talked through over several minutes, the draft sometimes puts the reasoning in the assessment and only part of the decision in the plan, or leaves a follow-up interval in the body of the note. Before signing they read the plan against what they remember deciding and move or add items by hand. They put it at "a couple of times on a full clinic day", an informal impression, not a count.
[HIGH] (medication changes) They enter medication orders themselves, so they know what they decided; the question at sign-off is whether the note says the same thing. Their main check is that every medication change in the plan matches the order they placed, and that it is written as a decision. When the draft words a change tentatively, as it was discussed rather than as it was decided, they rewrite it. They said they make this check on every medication line, underlined or not.
[MEDIUM] (sound-alike names) They recalled one sound-alike drug name since GA, glyburide written where glipizide had been said, and said it was underlined. It is one recollection, not a rate; the GA release-candidate round records sound-alike names as a known, monitored error type (2026-01-13-usability-test-ambient-scribe-ga-release-candidate/session-notes.md:31). They said they would check medication lines against the order whether or not anything marked them, because a wrong name can be heard confidently.
Representative Quotes
"I put the order in myself, so I know what I decided. The question is whether the note says the same thing." — Physician (Family Medicine), P147
"'We talked about lowering the dose' isn't a plan. I change it to what we actually did." — Physician (Family Medicine), P147
Recommendations
Share with the ambient scribe team that decisions made during the visit, especially medication changes and follow-up intervals, need to reach the plan section, worded as decisions.
When drafts are evaluated, check the plan section's completeness against what was decided in the visit, not only transcription accuracy.
When the distinct medication flag's design is next reviewed, note that this physician checks every medication line against the order regardless of marking; whether a flag would change that is untested.
Follow-ups / Open Questions
How often plan items land outside the plan section is not measured; "a couple of times on a full clinic day" is one physician's impression.
Whether NPs and PAs, or other physicians, check the plan and medication lines the same way is not known; this is one interview.
Whether the distinct medication flag would change how signers check medication lines is untested; it has not shipped.

Method
Method: 1:1 interview, 45 min
Researcher: Priya Patel
Full participant roster: see participants.md in this folder
Context: The participant is a nurse practitioner in an ambulatory primary care clinic, about five years in that role. They use the ambient scribe for most visits. Exam rooms in their clinic have a workstation that clinicians share across the day, signing in with a badge tap. The idle timeout is 10 minutes and is not adjustable per feature (2026-02-17-session-lock-during-dictation/session-notes.md:49-50). This is an interview about their own practice; nothing was shown or observed.
Key Findings
[HIGH] (lock during a visit) A lock happens to them when they step away from the workstation to the exam table within the room, typically for the physical exam, and the idle timeout fires while the scribe is listening. When they come back the widget looks frozen and shows no message. Their practice is to re-authenticate and scroll through the draft to see what is still there before they say anything more. They described learning this after re-dictating a visit summary early on and then finding the original draft intact; that is their account of their own practice, not an observed change. They do not know what happens to their in-progress draft if a colleague signs in on that workstation while their session is locked, and they did not want to find out with a patient's visit. So they stop the scribe before leaving a room, even mid-visit, and start it again when they return. That avoids the question but splits one visit across several recordings, which they then have to read as one draft. How the product behaves in that case is not recorded in the corpus and was not settled here.

Add the shared exam-room workstation to the review of the paused-state recovery flow: what a clinician sees after a lock when a colleague has signed in on the same workstation.
Make sure the paused-state message says whose draft is preserved, not only that a draft is.
When the paused state ships, re-test whether clinicians still stop the scribe before leaving a shared room, as well as whether they still re-dictate.

What happens to an in-progress draft when another clinician signs in on the same workstation during a lock is not recorded in the corpus and was not settled here.
How often locks interrupt a visit is not measured; "most afternoons, at least once" is one nurse practitioner's impression.

raw:2026-05-12-interview-cdi-specialist-.excerpt:
Objective
Understand how scribe-drafted notes have changed clinical documentation integrity (CDI) review since the ambient scribe went GA in January 2026, and how a CDI specialist would want the AI coding-suggestion concept (July 2025 prototype, not built or piloted) to behave when the documentation behind a code is incomplete.
Method
Method: 1:1 interview, 45 min
Researcher: Priya Patel
Full participant roster: see participants.md in this folder
Context: Participant does concurrent and retrospective CDI review on inpatient and some outpatient encounters and writes physician queries. They work alongside the coding team but sit in a separate queue.
Key Findings
[HIGH] (documentation gaps) Scribe-drafted notes are fluent and well organized, so they read as complete. What's missing (acuity, severity, the clinical indicators that support a diagnosis, the link between conditions) is harder to spot than in a sparse typed note, where a gap was obvious at a glance. They said a scribe-drafted note now takes a more deliberate read, by their own informal count a few extra minutes per note, because they can no longer rely on a note "looking thin" to tell them where to look.
[MEDIUM] (queries) Wants the coding-suggestion concept to suggest queries, not codes, when the documentation is incomplete. Their worry is that a suggested code on an under-specified note pushes the coder either to an unspecified code or toward a leading query. They'd want a draft query that states the clinical indicators found and asks the physician to clarify, in non-leading language Compliance has approved.
[LOW] (workflow) There is no hand-off signal between CDI and coding. Coders can't see that a CDI query is already open on an encounter, so an encounter sometimes gets coded before the answer comes back, or the physician gets a second, near-duplicate query from the coder. They described this as an annoyance that predates the scribe, not something GA caused.
Representative Quotes
"The note sounds finished. That's the problem. It reads like a really good note, and then you go looking for the acuity and it's just not in there." — Clinical Documentation Integrity Specialist, P123
"Don't hand me a code. Hand me the question I should be asking the doctor." — Clinical Documentation Integrity Specialist, P123
Recommendations
For under-specified documentation, have the coding-suggestion concept output a draft query routed to CDI instead of a code, with query wording reviewed by Compliance so it stays non-leading.
Share CDI's list of the specificity elements most often missing from scribe-drafted notes with the ambient scribe team, alongside the coders' list.
Separately from any AI work, look at a simple "query open" indicator on the encounter that coders can see.
Follow-ups / Open Questions
Confirm with Compliance which query templates are already approved, and whether AI-drafted query text would need its own review.
Get CDI query counts for the months before and after GA.

raw:2026-05-28-interview-icu-nurse-hando.title: Interview — ICU Nurse on the Handoff Narrative
raw:2026-05-28-interview-icu-nurse-hando.excerpt:
Objective
The February 2025 nursing survey's top volunteered concern was losing the clinical narrative voice, and an ICU respondent wrote that their notes are how they hand off a patient safely. This session asked an ICU nurse what the narrative in their notes does at shift handoff, and what they would expect of AI drafting nursing notes, which doesn't exist.
Method
Method: 1:1 interview, 45 min
Researcher: Priya Patel
Full participant roster: see participants.md in this folder
Context: The participant is a senior registered nurse in an adult ICU. Their charting is manual; the ambient scribe, GA since January 2026, drafts notes for physicians, NPs and PAs only, and no nurse uses it for their own documentation. Everything they said about AI drafting nursing notes is an expectation, not experience. They did not take part in any earlier session; they are not P07, the ICU nurse quoted in the February 2025 survey.
Key Findings
[HIGH] (handoff narrative) The narrative part of their note is a safety artifact: it is where they record what worried them and why, the trend they are watching, and what they would do if it got worse. Flowsheet values show what happened; the narrative shows what the next nurse should watch for. At handoff the oncoming nurse reads it before the verbal report, and they described it as the one part of the note they write for a specific reader.
[MEDIUM] (expectation of AI drafting) They were skeptical of any AI drafting nursing notes. Their expectation was that a draft could summarise the flowsheet but would not know what they were worried about, and that a nurse at the end of a twelve-hour shift would accept it rather than rewrite it. They saw that as worse than writing less. This is an expectation of a tool that doesn't exist.
[LOW] (where help might fit) They could see help with the parts that repeat flowsheet data in prose, as long as the narrative stayed theirs. This came up once, unprompted, and wasn't explored.
Representative Quotes
"The numbers are in the flowsheet. My note is what I was worried about at three a.m. That's what the next nurse needs." — Registered Nurse (ICU), P140
"At hour twelve, if it hands me a paragraph, I'm going to sign it. That's what scares me." — Registered Nurse (ICU), P140
Recommendations
Treat the nursing narrative as a handoff safety artifact in any future discussion of AI drafting for nurses, not only as a documentation-burden item.
If AI drafting for nursing notes is ever scoped, test end-of-shift acceptance of drafts directly, since this nurse's concern was about tired nurses accepting a draft, not about accuracy.
Follow-ups / Open Questions
This is one ICU nurse. It is consistent with the February 2025 survey's note that ICU and ED nurses were more skeptical, but one interview does not validate that unit-level claim, which was low-confidence and had no per-unit figures.
Whether skepticism varies with years of experience (the survey's tenure question) is still open; this interview can't answer it.
How nurses on other units use the narrative at handoff is not known.

raw:2026-06-16-interview-utilization-rev.excerpt:
Objective
Check the prior-auth scope decision in prior-authorization.md against daily work, with a nurse who now uses the drafting panel. The finding says scope discipline held: pilot scope was limited to "straightforward" cases and complex cases were kept out ( findings/prior-authorization.md :35-38), and that inline citations are actively used rather than ignored (lines 32-34). Both rest on test sessions with realistic scenarios. The participant is P19, returning from 2025-04-08-usability-test-prior-auth-ai-v1, where they said they liked the draft "for the boring, obvious cases" and wanted it kept away from complicated ones. The questions were whether the straightforward boundary matches the cases that actually reach them, how they check the panel's citations, and which cases they still do by hand.
Method
Method: 1:1 interview, 45 min
Researcher: Priya Patel
Full participant roster: see participants.md in this folder
Context: A limited pilot of the prior-auth drafting panel has run in the utilization review department since early 2026, on straightforward cases only, the scope the v2 test recommended (2025-11-04-usability-test-prior-auth-ai-v2/session-notes.md:39). Complex cases stay manual. The pilot is not generally available and has not reached other departments. The panel shows inline citations to the chart entries behind each part of the draft. The participant is in the pilot and uses the panel on their own straightforward cases. They took part in the April 2025 v1 test only, not the November 2025 v2 test, so nothing here speaks to v2. They are not P17, the utilization review supervisor quoted in v1 and v2. No pilot outcomes data was reviewed in this session, and the written straightforward-case definition was not reviewed either; what the participant says about it is their own description.
Key Findings
[HIGH] (boundary vs case mix) The boundary holds as a rule but does not sort their cases cleanly up front. In their own words, a straightforward case is "one request, one current diagnosis, criteria we see every week." On their informal estimate, roughly half of what reaches them in a week looks like that at intake, and some of those turn out not to be once they are into the chart: an older related request, a prior claim denial on the same service, or evidence spread over years of notes. When that happens they stop using the draft and finish the case by hand, so the decision is made case by case, partway through, by the nurse. This complicates the finding's "scope discipline held" claim: the scope held in testing, where cases were labelled straightforward or complex in advance, but in daily work the label is not known until the nurse has read enough of the chart.
[MEDIUM] (citation checking) They open the citations for the diagnosis and for the date of the most recent supporting note on every case, and skim the rest. They check dates first because of the outdated-code issue they saw in v1. They said they have not seen an outdated code in the pilot; that is their account, not a count, and v2's no-recurrence result covered 4 test cases. This confirms the finding's claim that citations are used rather than ignored, and extends it from a test session to one nurse's daily use; it says nothing about how other pilot users check.
[MEDIUM] (manual cases) Cases they still do entirely by hand: anything following a prior claim denial, requests covering several services at once, and cases with long histories where they have to judge which evidence matters. Their reason was the same for all three: the work is deciding what to include, and a draft that includes things they then have to remove is slower than starting blank. Their rule when unsure is to treat the case as complex.
Representative Quotes
"The definition's fine on paper. The trouble is a lot of my cases look straightforward right up until I'm into the chart." — Utilization Review Nurse, P19 (returning from 2025-04-08-usability-test-prior-auth-ai-v1)
"I click the dates first. After the old-codes problem last year, I don't trust a diagnosis until I've seen when it was written." — Utilization Review Nurse, P19 (returning from 2025-04-08-usability-test-prior-auth-ai-v1)
Recommendations
When prior-authorization.md is next revised, say that the straightforward boundary is applied by the nurse during the case, not only at intake, and that cases leave the draft partway through.
Treat a case that starts in the panel and moves to manual as a normal path, and ask the pilot team whether it is recorded, since it is part of what the pilot is testing.
Keep dates prominent in the citations; this nurse checks them before anything else.
Follow-ups / Open Questions
How the pilot is performing is not known: no outcomes data (time, accuracy, claim denials) is recorded in the corpus, and none was reviewed here. The only time figures on record are v1's estimate and v2's measurement on 2 straightforward test cases.
What "pilot expansion" in the v2 recommendation meant (how many nurses, how many weeks, what go/no-go metric) is still the open question v2 left; this participant did not know, and was not in v2.
How often a case leaves the draft partway through is not measured; "roughly half" looking straightforward at intake is one nurse's estimate.
Whether other pilot users check citations the same way is not known; this is one interview.

They put a long list at "fifteen lines, give or take" for many of their patients, an informal impression, not a count.
[HIGH] (dose schedules) In their account, dose changes in their clinic are often schedules rather than a single number: a prednisone taper stepped down over several weeks, or methotrexate taken once a week, where the day matters. They said the draft sometimes keeps the first step of a taper and drops the rest, or writes the methotrexate dose without "weekly". Those lines are usually not underlined, because each word was heard clearly. They rewrite the schedule by hand before signing. They put an incomplete taper at "a few times a month", an informal impression.
[MEDIUM] (whose dose) Patients often say what they actually take, which can differ from what was prescribed ("I've been taking half"). The draft records the dose that was said without saying who said it, so a patient's report can read like the clinician's decision. They check whether each dose in the draft is what the patient reported or what they decided, and reword it so the note says which. This is one rheumatologist's practice; whether other clinicians make the same check is not known.
[LOW] (what would help) Asked what would help, without being shown anything, they said a way to see which medication lines changed at this visit. That is an expectation; nothing was shown, and the distinct medication flag was not discussed with them.
Representative Quotes
"Fifteen medications and one of them changed today. The draft doesn't tell me which one, so I read all fifteen." — Physician (Rheumatology), P149
"It got the first dose right. The rest of the taper just isn't there." — Physician (Rheumatology), P149
Recommendations
Share with the ambient scribe team that, in this rheumatologist's account, multi-step dose schedules (tapers, weekly dosing) are where medication lines go wrong without being underlined, because each word is heard clearly.
When drafts are evaluated, include specialty-clinic visits with long medication lists and multi-step dose schedules, not only single dose changes.
Explore, as an open design question, whether a draft could show which medication lines changed at this visit and whether a dose is the patient's report or the clinician's decision; neither has been designed or tested.
Follow-ups / Open Questions
How often a dose schedule is written incompletely is not measured; "a few times a month" is one rheumatologist's impression.
Whether other specialists, or NPs and PAs in specialty clinics, check medication lines the same way is not known; this is one interview.
Whether the distinct medication flag, which targets sound-alike names, would help with dose schedules is untested; it has not shipped.

Objective
The September 2025 baseline survey asked about after-hours charting and reported it for physician respondents (2025-09-09-survey-clinician-burnout-documentation-burden-baseline/session-notes.md:29). It recommended future re-surveys "(e.g., 6 and 12 months post-rollout)" (same file, :40) and listed as a follow-up "a repeat of this exact survey instrument 6 months after ambient scribe GA rollout" (same file, :44). No repeat is recorded in research/raw on or before this session's date: the only survey folder after September 2025 is the December 2025 all-staff AI readiness pulse (2025-12-02-survey-allstaff-ai-readiness-pulse). No earlier 1:1 session asked a physician about charting after clinic: among raw sessions dated on or before 2026-07-02, after-hours and "pajama time" charting appear only in the September survey (session-notes.md:29, :40). This session asked a family physician, about six months after the January 2026 GA, when and how they finish their notes now. It is one physician's informal account and does not re-measure anything the survey measured.
Method
Method: 1:1 interview, 45 min
Researcher: Priya Patel
Full participant roster: see participants.md in this folder
Context: The participant is a family medicine physician in an ambulatory primary care clinic, about ten years in practice. They opted in to the ambient scribe shortly after the January 2026 GA and use it for most visits. The scribe drafts the visit note only; the clinician reviews the draft, corrects single lines in place, and signs, and enters orders separately. They did not take part in any earlier session; whether they responded to the September 2025 survey is not known, because it was anonymous. This is an interview about their own practice; nothing was shown or observed, and nothing was timed.
Key Findings
[MEDIUM] (evening notes) They still finish some notes after clinic on most days. In their account the evening work is now mostly reading and signing drafts they didn't get to between visits, plus the notes for visits where they chose not to use the scribe; before the scribe, they recalled, it was mostly writing notes from memory. They put it at "four or five notes on a full day", an informal estimate. They have not timed it, then or now, and this is not a measure of time saved.
[MEDIUM] (which notes wait) The drafts that wait until the evening are the ones that need more than a quick read: long visits with several problems, and drafts where they expect to move or rewrite lines. Short visits they try to sign straight after the patient leaves. When the clinic runs late, that falls apart and more drafts wait.
[MEDIUM] (reviewing later) Reviewing a draft hours after the visit is harder for them than reviewing it straight away, because checking it depends on remembering what was said. In the evening they read more slowly and leave more of it as written when they can't recall the detail. That is their own description of their practice; how often it happens was not discussed.
[LOW] (other evening work) They said much of their evening now goes to patient messages and test results rather than notes, and the scribe doesn't touch those. That is their impression; how their evening time divides was not measured.
Representative Quotes
"The evening used to be writing. Now it's mostly reading what it wrote and signing, and then the messages." — Physician (Family Medicine), P150
"Right after the visit I remember what we said. By the evening I'm checking it against a memory that's gone fuzzy." — Physician (Family Medicine), P150
Recommendations
Treat this interview as context for the repeat of the September 2025 survey, not as a measure. Whether after-hours charting has changed since GA needs that repeat, which the baseline recommended and which is not recorded in the corpus.
Share with the ambient scribe team that, in this physician's account, a draft reviewed hours after the visit gets a weaker check, because the check depends on memory of the visit.
In later after-hours questions, ask about patient messages and test results as well as notes, since this physician placed much of their evening work there.
Follow-ups / Open Questions
Whether after-hours charting has changed since GA is not measured; this is one physician's informal account, and no repeat of the September 2025 survey is recorded in the corpus.
How their evening time divides between notes, messages and results is not measured.
Whether other physicians, or NPs and PAs, describe the same pattern is not known; this is one interview.

raw:2026-07-07-interview-care-coordinato.excerpt:
Objective
Get a reaction to the override-reason capture screens ( wireflows/alert-triage-override-reason-capture.md ) from a coordinator who asked for exactly this kind of capture. The participant is P81, returning from 2025-08-26-usability-test-alert-triage-ai-care-coordination (August 2025); this interview is in July 2026. In that test they said they wanted to tell the ranking "this one's more urgent because I know this patient's history" and had nowhere to put it. The question was whether the reason list and the flow fit the reasons they actually have.
Method
Method: 1:1 interview, 45 min
Researcher: Priya Patel
Full participant roster: see participants.md in this folder
Context: The participant reacted to the in-review wireflow screens: the "Override" action on a ranked queue item, the reason-capture modal (patient-history risk / recency not clinically relevant / other + free text) and the skip-reason branch. The wireflow is designed and in review, not built, and the AI-ranked queue hasn't been built; their team still works the chronological queue.
Key Findings
[HIGH] (reason list) Their most common reason for moving an alert is something the patient or a family member said on the phone that isn't in the chart yet. That reason isn't in the list. Looking at the screens, they said they would pick "other" most of the time, so the reason the capture most needs to collect would land in the least useful bucket.
[MEDIUM] (effort) They would give a reason if it took one tap. They would not type free text on every override, and expected that on a busy day they would skip the modal rather than type. This is what they said they would do; nothing was observed in use.
[MEDIUM] (feedback loop) If they never saw any effect from the reasons they gave, they said they would stop giving them after a while. The wireflow logs reasons for model-tuning review and doesn't show coordinators anything back.
Representative Quotes
"Half the time it's something the daughter told me on the phone yesterday. That's not in the chart yet, and it's not on your list, so I'd be hitting 'other' all day." — Care Coordinator, P81 (returning from 2025-08-26-usability-test-alert-triage-ai-care-coordination)
"One tap, fine. But if I never see it change anything, I'll stop bothering." — Care Coordinator, P81 (returning from 2025-08-26-usability-test-alert-triage-ai-care-coordination)
Recommendations
Add a one-tap reason for information from the patient or family that isn't in the chart yet, before the wireflow leaves review.
Keep every reason one tap, with free text optional, so a busy coordinator doesn't skip the modal altogether.
Decide how coordinators will see that their reasons are used, and say so in the design.
Follow-ups / Open Questions
How often overrides would fall under "other" with the current list is not known; this is one coordinator's expectation.
Whether a feedback loop would keep coordinators giving reasons is untested.
How the 2025 ranking weighted its inputs, and how accurate it is, are still not documented.

raw:2026-08-04-interview-care-coordinato.excerpt:
Objective
Understand where alert noise comes from for a coordinator on a high-risk panel, and whether AI ranking addresses it, following up the August 2025 alert-triage test and the May 2026 supervisor's estimate that many alerts are administrative rather than clinical.
Method
Method: 1:1 interview, 45 min
Researcher: Priya Patel
Full participant roster: see participants.md in this folder
Context: The participant is a care coordinator on a complex care team with a high-risk panel. Their team works the chronological queue; the AI-ranked queue hasn't been built. They reacted to a description of the ranked queue, not to screens. They did not take part in any earlier session.
Key Findings
[HIGH] (repeat alerts) For them, the main source of noise is repeat alerts for the same patient, more than the order the alerts come in. They would want alerts grouped by patient before any ranking is applied, so that they deal with one patient once rather than meeting them several times down the queue. This is their account; no queue data was reviewed in this session.
[MEDIUM] (patient history) Their judgement of a patient's risk leans on knowing that patient's history, which a ranking based on the alert alone wouldn't have. This is a second voice alongside P81's 2025 comment about knowing a patient's history, from a different coordinator on a different kind of panel.
Representative Quotes
"It's not the order that gets me, it's seeing the same patient four times. Put them together first, then rank them if you want." — Care Coordinator (complex care), P134
"I know these patients. Half of deciding who's at risk is knowing what happened to them last winter." — Care Coordinator (complex care), P134
Recommendations
Explore grouping alerts by patient as a step before ranking, and test it with coordinators on high-risk panels.
Keep patient history in view when ranking signals are next revisited, in line with the August 2025 recommendation.

How many alerts are repeats for the same patient is not measured; this is one coordinator's account.
How the 2025 ranking was built and how accurate it is are still not documented, and whether the override-capture idea reached the data-science team isn't recorded.
