raw:2026-09-15-interview-infusion-nurse-.title: Interview — Infusion Nurse on Medication Changes in Scribe-Drafted Notes
raw:2026-09-15-interview-infusion-nurse-.excerpt:
Objective
The medication thread in ambient-scribe-post-ga-refinements.md rests on a concept test of a distinct sound-alike medication flag with the people who review and sign scribe drafts: physicians and NPs (2026-02-10-ambient-scribe-medication-flag-concept/participants.md). Nobody who reads a signed, scribe-drafted note and then gives the medication has been asked about it. This session asked an infusion nurse how they check medication changes in the treating provider's visit note before they administer, and what, if anything, they see on medication lines in a signed note.
Method
Method: 1:1 interview, 45 min
Researcher: Priya Patel
Full participant roster: see participants.md in this folder
Context: The participant is a registered nurse in an ambulatory infusion clinic, mid-career. Patients come in for scheduled infusions, and before starting one the nurse checks the infusion order against the treating provider's most recent visit note, which since the January 2026 GA is often scribe-drafted. The scribe drafts visit notes for physicians, NPs and PAs only; the participant doesn't use it, and their own charting is manual. They did not take part in any earlier session. They are not P138, the primary care clinic nurse interviewed in March 2026, and they don't do care coordination or post-discharge calls. The distinct medication flag is recorded in the corpus as a concept test (2026-02-10) and a wireframe in review ( wireframes/ambient-scribe-medication-flag.md ), whose hover copy reads "verify before signing"; nothing was shown in this session.
Key Findings
[HIGH] (checking before administering) Before every infusion they compare the order with the treating provider's latest visit note, looking for a medication change: a changed dose, a held infusion, a premedication added or stopped, or a lab value that has to be checked first. They give the medication from the order, not the note; the note is how they find out whether the order still reflects what was decided at the visit. When the two disagree, they hold the infusion and contact the provider before starting. In scribe-drafted notes they sometimes find a change in the body of the note, written up from the conversation, rather than in the plan, or worded so that they can't tell whether it was decided ("we'll probably bring the dose down"). They recalled holding an infusion to check for this reason "maybe once or twice a month" since GA; that is an informal recollection, not a count, and they couldn't say how many of those came from the scribe's drafting and how many from the provider. This is the same pattern of plan items landing in the body that the March 2026 clinic nurse described (2026-03-17-interview-clinic-nurse-reading-scribe-drafted-notes/session-notes.md:30), in a different setting: here the cost is a delayed infusion before administration, not a delayed callback.
[MEDIUM] (the flag and readers) The medication flag has so far been designed and tested for the person signing the note. This nurse reads the note after it is signed and acts on its medication lines. In the signed notes they read, they said they have not seen any marking on medication lines, neither a flag nor an underline; that is what they see, not a statement of how the product behaves. Their working assumption is that every medication line in a signed note was checked by the provider. That is a reader's version of the over-trust risk the concept test found in 2 of 6 signers, who trusted unflagged lines more: a reader who never sees a flag treats every signed line as checked. They said that if a line had been flagged and the provider then confirmed or changed it, they would want to know, because that is the line they would check against the order first. That is an expectation; no such view exists. This extends the medication-flag finding to readers who didn't write the note.
Representative Quotes
"I don't hang anything off the note, I hang it off the order. The note is how I find out if the order's still right." — Registered Nurse (infusion clinic), P143
"If it's signed, I assume they checked the meds. I've never seen anything on a med line that tells me different." — Registered Nurse (infusion clinic), P143
Recommendations
Share with the ambient scribe team that medication changes decided at the visit need to reach the plan section as decided changes, because infusion nurses check them against the order before administering.
When the medication flag's design is next reviewed, include nurses who read signed notes and give the medication as a user group, and decide explicitly whether anything about a flag, and what the signer did with it, should reach them. Don't assume either answer.
Keep this evidence separate from the care coordination evidence on after-visit summaries: this is the visit note checked against the order before administration, not the summary a patient takes home.
Follow-ups / Open Questions
Whether the medication flag, or any confidence marking, stays visible after a note is signed is not recorded in the corpus and was not settled here. This nurse has not seen any marking on signed notes, which says what they see, not how the product behaves; and the corpus records the distinct flag only as a concept test and a wireframe in review.

raw:2026-09-17-interview-utilization-rev.title: Interview — Utilization Review Nurse on Checking Citations
raw:2026-09-17-interview-utilization-rev.excerpt:
Objective
prior-authorization.md says nurses want inline citations to the chart text behind each part of the draft, and that in v2 the citations were used rather than ignored, with 3 of 4 participants clicking into at least one citation before accepting ( findings/prior-authorization.md :30-34). Both claims come from the April 2025 v1 and November 2025 v2 tests, whose participants asked for the citations or tested them. This session asked a utilization review nurse who joined the department after both tests, and has only ever used the panel in the pilot, whether they want the citations and how they check them, and how they handle the cases the panel doesn't take, including claim denials and calls with the health plan.
Method
Method: 1:1 interview, 45 min
Researcher: Priya Patel
Full participant roster: see participants.md in this folder
Context: A limited pilot of the prior-auth drafting panel has run in the utilization review department since early 2026, on straightforward cases only; complex cases stay manual. The pilot is not generally available and has not reached other departments. The panel shows inline citations to the chart entries behind each part of the draft. The participant joined the department after the November 2025 v2 test and did not take part in any earlier session, so nothing here speaks to v1 or v2. They use the panel on their own straightforward cases. They are not P19, the utilization review nurse from v1 and June 2026, and not P17, the utilization review supervisor from v1 and v2. No pilot outcomes data was reviewed in this session, and the written straightforward-case definition was not reviewed either.
Key Findings
[MEDIUM] (citations as the way to read a draft) They want the citations, and don't think of them as an added feature: they have never used a draft without them, and opening them is how they read a draft at all. On each case they open the citation behind every criterion the request has to meet and read the chart entry it points to. What they check is whether that entry says what the draft says it says, not only that it exists; their example was a cited note that supports a symptom the draft describes as ongoing, when the note is months old. On their informal impression, most drafts need no change after checking and some need a sentence reworded; they kept no count. This confirms prior-authorization.md :30-34 for a nurse who wasn't in v1 or v2: the citations are wanted and used in pilot work, not only in testing. It also complicates the v2 measure: "clicked into at least one citation" records that a citation was opened, not what the nurse checked once it was.
[MEDIUM] (manual cases, claim denials and calls) Cases outside the pilot's straightforward scope they do by hand from the start. For a request that follows a claim denial, they begin from the denial letter's stated reason and then gather the chart evidence that answers it; in their view a draft built from the chart would start in the wrong place, because the reason is in the letter, not the chart. Before a call with the health plan about a case, they prepare by hand too, keeping their own list of chart references to have open during the call. They described the calls as the hardest part of the week to plan for, but gave no time figure. For a straightforward case that the health plan later asks about, they said they find the evidence again from scratch; they didn't know whether a submitted request keeps the panel's citations.
Representative Quotes
"I've never had a draft without them. The citations aren't extra, they're how I read the thing." — Utilization Review Nurse, P144
"A denial comes with a reason, and the reason's in the letter, not the chart. So I start from the letter and go find what answers it." — Utilization Review Nurse, P144
Recommendations
When prior-authorization.md is next revised, note that the citation requirement holds for a nurse who joined during the pilot, and that what they check is whether the cited text supports the draft's wording.
If citation use is measured in the pilot, record what nurses check in a citation, not only whether they open one.
Ask the pilot team whether a submitted request keeps its citations, so a nurse can reuse them if the health plan asks about the case later.
Follow-ups / Open Questions
How the pilot is performing is not known: no outcomes data (time, accuracy, claim denials) is recorded in the corpus, none was reviewed here, and the participant had not seen any figures. The only time figures on record are v1's estimate and v2's measurement on 2 straightforward test cases.
Whether a submitted request keeps its citations is not known; the participant didn't know.
How many drafts need changing after the citations are checked is not counted; "most" needing no change is one nurse's impression.
Whether other pilot users check citations the same way is not known; this is one interview.
Whether drafting could help with requests that follow a claim denial is untested; the participant does them by hand, and nothing here supports bringing them into the pilot.

raw:2026-09-22-interview-returning-inter.excerpt:
Objective
The participant is P09, returning from 2026-01-13-usability-test-ambient-scribe-ga-release-candidate. In the v0.1 test they said they had to read every word anyway (2025-02-25-usability-test-ambient-scribe-v01/session-notes.md:36-37). In the v0.2 test they said they still read every line, and that getting it right once didn't mean they trusted it yet (2025-09-23-usability-test-ambient-scribe-v02/session-notes.md:36-37). At the GA release-candidate round they said it was the first time they had skimmed a section instead of reading every word, because it showed them where to look (2026-01-13-usability-test-ambient-scribe-ga-release-candidate/session-notes.md:36-37); that round recorded 4 of 6 participants saying the per-line underline let them skim high-confidence lines (same file, :30). This interview is in September 2026. The questions were what they edit in drafts now, what they read in full and what they skim, and what in their account has changed or stayed the same since January.
Method
Method: 1:1 interview, 45 min
Researcher: Priya Patel
Full participant roster: see participants.md in this folder
Context: The participant is an internal medicine physician in an ambulatory clinic. They have used the ambient scribe since the January 2026 GA. The scribe drafts the visit note only; they review the draft, correct single lines in place, and sign. Low-confidence transcription is shown with a subtle underline. Their earlier sessions were moderated usability tests; this is an interview about their own practice, nothing was shown or observed, and what they describe can't be compared directly with what those tests recorded. The researcher did not share what other participants had said.
Key Findings
[HIGH] (order of events) In their account, most of their edits now are not misheard words. The draft sometimes gets the order of events in the history wrong: which symptom came first, or how long ago something started. Those lines are usually not underlined, because each word was heard clearly. They put it at "a few notes most weeks", an informal impression, not a count.
[MEDIUM] (what they skim) They still skim history sections where nothing is underlined on routine follow-up visits, and read the assessment and plan in full on every draft. In January they said they skimmed a section for the first time instead of reading every word, because it showed them where to look (2026-01-13-usability-test-ambient-scribe-ga-release-candidate/session-notes.md:36); what they read in full that day is not recorded, so the two can't be compared line by line.
[MEDIUM] (new problems) After catching, during review in the spring, a draft whose history put two symptoms in the wrong order with nothing underlined, they began reading the whole history whenever a visit is about a new problem. That is their account of a change in their own practice since January, not an observed change.
[MEDIUM] (trust by section) Asked whether they trust the scribe more than in January, they said it depends on the section: they rely on it to have heard the words, and they check that the history and the plan say what happened and what they decided. They did not describe their trust as having grown overall, and this interview does not measure trust.
[LOW] (edit count) They put their edits at "one or two on most notes", an informal estimate.
Representative Quotes
"It hears the words. What I check is whether the story's in the right order." — Physician, Internal Medicine, P09 (returning from 2026-01-13-usability-test-ambient-scribe-ga-release-candidate)
"Do I trust it more than in January? For some sections. Not the plan, and not the history of a new problem." — Physician, Internal Medicine, P09 (returning from 2026-01-13-usability-test-ambient-scribe-ga-release-candidate)
Recommendations
Share with the ambient scribe team that, in this physician's account, the order of events in the history is where drafts go wrong without being underlined, because each word is heard clearly.
When drafts are evaluated, check the sequence of events in the history against the visit, not only word accuracy.
If the team wants to know whether review habits change over time, plan a measure for it; one returning participant's account can't show a trend.
Follow-ups / Open Questions
How often the order of events is wrong is not measured; "a few notes most weeks" is one physician's impression.
Whether other clinicians read the history in full for new problems is not known; this is one interview.
Whether skimming has changed since January is not measured; the January round was a moderated test and this is an interview.

raw:2026-10-08-interview-internal-medici.title: Interview — Internal Medicine Resident on Opting In to the Scribe
raw:2026-10-08-interview-internal-medici.excerpt:
Objective
The 2026-01-27 review of the internal analytics dashboard covering the first 4 weeks of GA-candidate rollout (2026-01-27-dashboard-review-ambient-scribe-ga-adoption/session-notes.md:26-27) found attending physicians opting in at a noticeably higher rate than residents in the same departments (same file, :37-39). It recommended a short follow-up interview round on the physician/resident adoption gap (same file, :44) and asked whether the gap is explained by workflow differences, trust, or something else, which dashboard data alone can't answer (same file, :47-48). No other raw session dated on or before this one mentions residents (the only matches are that file's :38, :44 and :47), and no earlier session interviewed a resident. This session asked one internal medicine resident, about nine months after the January 2026 GA, when and why they opted in to the ambient scribe. It is one resident's account and can't explain the gap the dashboard showed. Phase 4 has no inpatient, ED or behavioral health sessions, so whether and how residents use the scribe in those settings stays an open gap.
Method
Method: 1:1 interview, 45 min
Researcher: Priya Patel
Full participant roster: see participants.md in this folder
Context: The participant is an internal medicine resident who sees patients in an ambulatory internal medicine clinic on set half-days. They opted in to the ambient scribe in spring 2026, some months after the January 2026 GA, and use it for some of their clinic visits. The scribe drafts the visit note only; they review the draft, correct single lines in place, and sign. How attendings review resident notes was not discussed. Only clinic visits were discussed. They did not take part in any earlier session, and the researcher did not share what other participants had said. This is an interview about their own practice; nothing was shown or observed.
Key Findings
[MEDIUM] (waiting) They did not opt in at GA. In their account, writing their own notes in their first months in clinic was how they worked out their assessment of a patient, and they did not want a draft doing that for them while they were still learning it. They did not describe doubts about the draft's accuracy as the reason. This is one resident's reason; whether other residents waited for the same reason is not known.
[MEDIUM] (opting in) They opted in once they felt settled in writing notes and wanted to keep up on half-days that ran late. They put that at "about three months into clinic", an informal recollection.
[MEDIUM] (which visits) They use the scribe mostly for follow-up visits on problems they already know. For a new problem they write the assessment themselves, or rewrite the draft's assessment before signing. That is their description of their own practice; how often they do each was not discussed.
[LOW] (how they heard) What they knew about the scribe before opting in came from seeing attendings in their clinic use it. They did not know of any training or introduction aimed at residents.
Representative Quotes
"Writing the assessment is how I work out what I think. I didn't want something else writing it while I was still learning that." — Physician (Internal Medicine resident), P153
"For a follow-up on a problem I know, the draft is fine. A new problem, I still write the assessment myself." — Physician (Internal Medicine resident), P153
Recommendations
When resident adoption is next looked at, ask about note writing as part of training alongside workflow and trust; this resident's reason for waiting was learning to write notes, and they did not describe doubt about the draft's accuracy as a reason.
Interview more residents, including in other departments, before drawing conclusions about the adoption gap; this is one resident.
Record how residents are offered the scribe and any training for them; no raw session dated on or before this one records it.
Follow-ups / Open Questions
Why residents opted in at a lower rate than attendings in the first 4 weeks of GA-candidate rollout, as the dashboard review recorded (2026-01-27-dashboard-review-ambient-scribe-ga-adoption/session-notes.md:27, :37-39), is still not known; one resident's account can't explain it.
Whether residents use the scribe in inpatient, ED or behavioral health settings is not known; Phase 4 has no sessions in those settings, and the gap stays open.
How attendings review scribe-drafted resident notes was not discussed, and no raw session dated on or before this one records it.
